notes: Replaced vault-single-value-encryption with vault-encrypt-string-stdin-input to avoid testing both sides of encryption granularity. Replaced vault-view-disk-state with vault-password-client-label-argument to avoid a name giveaway.

cards.statement: Ansible applies a block's `when` condition separately before each task in that block.
cards.explanation: Ansible reevaluates the inherited condition for each enclosed task.

cards.statement: A block can repeat its complete task list for each item supplied to the block's `loop`.
cards.explanation: Ansible rejects loop as a block directive.
cards.misconception: Blocks support a loop directive.

cards.statement: A rescue task can inspect the failed task's return data through `ansible_failed_result`.
cards.explanation: ansible_failed_result holds the triggering task's captured result for rescue tasks.

cards.statement: Ansible runs a block's `always` tasks after a task in `rescue` returns `failed`.
cards.explanation: A task failure in rescue still permits execution of the block's always section.

cards.statement: Ansible continues the play on a host after its `rescue` tasks successfully handle a block failure.
cards.explanation: Successful rescue clears the original task's failed status and keeps the host executing the play.

cards.statement: Ansible starts a block's `rescue` section when a task reports its host as unreachable.
cards.explanation: Ansible excludes unreachable hosts from a block's rescue processing.
cards.misconception: Unreachable hosts trigger rescue.

cards.statement: After a task fails outside a block, Ansible continues that host's subsequent play tasks.
cards.explanation: Ansible stops further play tasks on the failed host by default, while other hosts continue.
cards.misconception: Ansible continues ordinary tasks on a host after an unhandled failure.

cards.statement: With `ignore_errors: true`, Ansible keeps an unreachable host active for later tasks.
cards.explanation: ignore_errors handles task failures. Use ignore_unreachable to keep scheduling tasks for a host reported unreachable.
cards.misconception: ignore_errors also ignores unreachable-host status.

cards.statement: Ansible marks a task failed when any condition in a `failed_when` list is true.
cards.explanation: A failed_when list uses implicit and, so the task fails when its listed conditions are true together.
cards.misconception: Ansible joins failed_when list entries with logical or.

cards.statement: `changed_when: false` makes Ansible report an otherwise successful command task as `ok`.
cards.explanation: The changed_when override alters the reported change status while the successful command still executes.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.17, Ansible runs `rescue` on every host after a block fails with `any_errors_fatal`.
cards.explanation: any_errors_fatal spreads the block's failure across hosts, so rescue also runs on hosts where the task succeeded.

cards.statement: With `serial`, Ansible aborts the play when a batch's failure percentage equals `max_fail_percentage`.
cards.explanation: A serial batch's failure percentage must exceed max_fail_percentage to abort the play; matching the threshold is insufficient.
cards.misconception: Reaching max_fail_percentage is enough to abort a play.

cards.statement: Ansible selects `main` as the task-file entry point when an included role uses the default `tasks_from`.
cards.explanation: include_role defaults tasks_from to main, selecting the role's task file with that entry name.

cards.statement: Ansible requires each standard role subdirectory to exist before loading a role.
cards.explanation: A role includes the directories it uses; unused standard directories are optional.
cards.misconception: Missing standard subdirectories make a role invalid.

cards.statement: Ansible favors `roles_path` over the playbook's `roles/` directory for a shared standalone role name.
cards.explanation: The playbook's adjacent roles/ directory takes priority over roles_path.
cards.misconception: roles_path outranks the playbook-adjacent roles directory.

cards.statement: Ansible runs roles listed under `roles:` after the play's `pre_tasks` have finished.
cards.explanation: The preliminary task phase completes before Ansible enters the play's statically listed roles.

cards.statement: Ansible executes dependencies from `meta/main.yml` before the role that declares them.
cards.explanation: Declared dependencies run first, placing prerequisites ahead of the declaring role's tasks.

cards.statement: Ansible runs identical `roles:` entries separately by default.
cards.explanation: Ansible deduplicates matching roles entries within one play unless the role enables allow_duplicates.
cards.misconception: Identical roles entries each cause a separate execution.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.include_role` keeps role vars and defaults within the role's scope by default.
cards.explanation: include_role defaults public to false, so later play tasks do not gain that role's vars and defaults.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.15, Ansible confines vars passed under a `roles:` entry to that role's scope.
cards.explanation: Inline vars supplied to a roles entry stay local rather than becoming play variables.

cards.statement: By default, Ansible validates role arguments from `meta/argument_specs.yml` while parsing the playbook.
cards.explanation: Ansible validates role arguments at the beginning of role execution, before its normal tasks.
cards.misconception: Role argument validation happens while parsing the playbook, before execution starts.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.include_tasks` repeats the included task group for each item when the include uses `loop`.
cards.explanation: Ansible processes the include for each loop item, loading and executing the task file again for that iteration.

cards.statement: Ansible evaluates `when` on `ansible.builtin.import_tasks` once before the imported task group starts.
cards.explanation: An imported when condition belongs to each imported task and is evaluated again before each task executes.
cards.misconception: An import's when condition is evaluated once for the whole imported group.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.import_playbook` imports another playbook as a task inside a play's `tasks` list.
cards.explanation: import_playbook belongs at the playbook's top level, where it imports a list of plays.
cards.misconception: import_playbook belongs inside a play's task list.

cards.statement: A task using `ansible.builtin.copy` keeps its module choice when another collection also provides `copy`.
cards.explanation: The namespace and collection in ansible.builtin.copy identify the builtin implementation, preventing a same-named module from taking its place.

cards.statement: Ansible uses a play's `collections` list to resolve unqualified filter names.
cards.explanation: The collections keyword sets the search order for modules and action plugins. A filter needs its FQCN to select content from a collection.
cards.misconception: The collections keyword also supplies the search path for filters.

cards.statement: A role automatically inherits the `collections` search list defined by its calling play.
cards.explanation: A play's collections list stays outside the role's search settings. Set the role's own collections list in its meta/main.yml.
cards.misconception: A play's collections search list flows into the roles it calls.

cards.statement: A role inside a collection automatically searches that collection first for a short module name.
cards.explanation: A role's containing collection leads its implicit search path, so tasks in the role can address that collection's modules by short name.

cards.statement: The Ansible docs recommend FQCNs over the `collections` keyword for references to collection content.
cards.explanation: The collections guide favors explicit module or plugin references over relying on a collections search list.

cards.statement: `ansible-galaxy collection install` places collections under `~/.ansible/collections` by default.
cards.explanation: The default collection destination belongs to the user running the installer; ansible-galaxy stores the collections beneath it.

cards.statement: `ansible-galaxy collection install` automatically replaces an installed collection with its newest version.
cards.explanation: Use --upgrade to request an installed collection's upgrade. An ordinary install retains a collection that already satisfies the requested version.
cards.misconception: A normal collection install refreshes an already installed collection to the newest available version.

cards.statement: `ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml` supports installing roles and collections from the same file.
cards.explanation: A requirements file can contain both roles and collections sections for one install invocation.

source.title: Installing roles and collections from the same requirements.yml file

cards.statement: A role's `requirements.yml` version entry supports ranges such as `>=1.0.0,<2.0.0`.
cards.explanation: Role requirements select a specific version. Comparison ranges apply to collection requirements.
cards.misconception: Role requirements accept the version-range syntax used by collection requirements.

cards.statement: `ansible-galaxy` uses supplied signatures to verify a collection installed from a local `tar.gz` file.
cards.explanation: Galaxy signature verification applies to collections obtained from distribution servers. Local tarball installs bypass user-provided signatures.
cards.misconception: User-provided signatures are checked for a local collection tarball installation.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.21, ansible-galaxy installs collections with incompatible `requires_ansible` for later validation.
cards.explanation: Galaxy excludes incompatible collection versions from installation by default, checking requires_ansible against the running ansible-core.
cards.misconception: Galaxy installs collections despite incompatible requires_ansible metadata and postpones the compatibility check.

cards.statement: The `ansible` community package bundles a curated collection set alongside the ansible-core runtime.
cards.explanation: Installing ansible supplies community-selected collections in addition to the core runtime and its builtin content.

cards.statement: Ansible Vault accepts standard input as the plaintext source for `ansible-vault encrypt_string`.
cards.explanation: Pipe the plaintext into encrypt_string; --stdin-name assigns the variable name for that input.

cards.statement: Whole-file Ansible Vault encryption conceals the variable names inside an encrypted vars file.
cards.explanation: Encrypting the entire variables file protects its names along with its values.

cards.statement: `ansible-vault rekey` rotates the password for a single encrypted value embedded in a plaintext YAML file.
cards.explanation: Individually encrypted variables need newly encrypted values for password rotation; rekey handles whole encrypted files.
cards.misconception: Rekey handles individually encrypted variables as well as whole encrypted files.

cards.statement: Ansible reads task definitions from a whole-file encrypted YAML task file when given its Vault password.
cards.explanation: Task definitions remain usable by Ansible when their source file has file-level Vault encryption.

cards.statement: `ansible-vault encrypt` accepts a binary file as input alongside Ansible's structured data files.
cards.explanation: File-level Vault encryption works on arbitrary file contents, including binary data.

cards.statement: `ansible-vault edit` returns an edited file to encrypted form when the operator closes the editor.
cards.explanation: The edit action decrypts a vaulted file for the editing session, then encrypts the saved contents again.

cards.statement: With `--vault-id prod@./vault-pass`, Ansible passes the `prod` label as an argument to that executable script.
cards.explanation: Ansible passes the label to password client scripts named with a -client or -client.EXTENSION suffix. The executable vault-pass receives no vault ID argument.
cards.misconception: Supplying a vault ID passes its label to any executable password-source script.

cards.statement: Ansible waits for a task to read a variable before decrypting a whole encrypted vars file.
cards.explanation: Ansible decrypts the whole encrypted file at load time, even if later tasks read just one variable from it.
cards.misconception: Ansible decrypts a whole variables file on demand for individual variable reads.

cards.statement: Ansible rejects a valid Vault password when its supplied vault ID label differs from the file's label.
cards.explanation: Vault ID labels are hints by default. A matching password decrypts content even when its supplied label differs.
cards.misconception: Ansible enforces matching vault ID labels with its default settings.

cards.statement: `--vault-id prod@prompt` makes Ansible ask the operator for a password tagged with the `prod` label.
cards.explanation: The part after @ selects the password source; prompt requests interactive entry for that vault ID.

cards.statement: Ansible tries an earlier password with a different vault ID before one matching the encrypted file's label.
cards.explanation: A supplied password whose label matches the encrypted content gets the first attempt, even when another password appears earlier on the command line.
cards.misconception: The supplied order takes priority over a password's matching vault ID label.

cards.statement: Ansible Vault stores an encrypted vault ID label beside the encrypted contents of a file.
cards.explanation: The vault ID label remains plain text in the header, making the label readable while the file's content stays encrypted.
cards.misconception: Vault encryption protects the vault ID label as part of the ciphertext.
